Le_Squish suggested canning which is a great idea. My sisters have both canned a variety of foods with success however I have been a bit intimidated by the process so freezing is my go-to method. Often I will make huge batches of sauce and freeze for use throughout the year. I do not notice the quality being affected by freezing. I make pizza sauce and red sauce and freeze it in ice cube trays so we can pull out however much we need and it doesn't take long to defrost. We make pizza close to once a week in the winter and I love the easy access for sauce. It doesn't have to be just red tomatoes either; pizza is so versatile!

Do you use a food strainer to get rid of the seeds and skin when making sauce? I ended up making some gazpacho the other week. The slicer tomatoes were easy enough to blanch, skin, and deseed. But I put the cherry tomatoes in a blender and used a wire mesh strainer to separate the skins and seeds, which was something of a chore. Also, do you put the cubes into a plastic bag after they are frozen, and if not does your sauce get freezer burned just sitting in the trays?

Ah gazpacho! What a wonderful use for garden vegetables!

It really depends on your personal taste preference for how you make the sauce. Using the strainer is (IMO) the best way to get an ultra-smooth sauce but it is a bit time consuming/ tedious. I grow Roma tomatoes for sauce because they have a lot of meat, few seeds and the skin is pretty easy to remove. Like you said, blanch the tomatoes so the skin splits and can be peeled off and then cut and remove the seeds. Finish up with a food processor. I am a bit pressed for time most of the time (due to shitty time-management skills lol) so a lot of times for smooth sauce I will just cut the tomatoes in half, remove the seeds and make the sauce. You will find the skin ends up curling into little flute-looking pieces that can be picked out easily. I still follow up with the food processor for the onion and garlic and whatnot. For chunky, like garden-vegetable sauce, I simply leave the skins on and seeds in because my family doesn't mind the texture and it saves a lot of time.

With huge batches I will move the frozen sauce cubes to freezer bags, trying to remove as much air as possible (you can use a straw to create a sort of vacuum-packed effect). In the event that there are a lot of ice crystals on the cubes, I just quickly rinse prior to defrosting and have never noticed the taste being affected. I also typically do have a few trays of cubes sitting in the upstairs freezer that I never bother to move to long-term storage and I just cover them with plastic wrap after filling so there is no air exposure and no freezer-burn.

I hope some of this info is useful because it has really been a game-changer for us to have easy access to healthy, homemade sauce throughout the year.
